whatItIs: A prose de-AI-ification skill that grew a measurement apparatus. Three layers: (1) a large prescriptive catalog — `references/patterns.md`, 95 KB, 87 `###` rules, a 112-entry tiered vocabulary table, P0/P1/P2 severity; (2) a dependency-free offline regex+stylometric engine, `detector/patterns.js`, 127 KB, 54 issue types (`TYPE_LABELS` at patterns.js:2421), emitting a 0-100 composite score; (3) an evaluation layer that measures the engine against a provenance-labelled corpus and publishes a null result against its own product. It also ships a 7-skill decomposition (`skills/avoid-ai-writing-router`, `preservation-verifier`, `voice-preserving-rewriter`, `file-edit-in-place`, `false-positive-reviewer`, `ai-writing-detector`) with a typed handoff envelope, plus Cursor-rule and OpenAI-plugin repackagings of the same text.
method: The skill proper (`skills/avoid-ai-writing/SKILL.md`, 21 KB) runs one of three modes — `rewrite` (default), `detect`, `edit` in-place — after mandatorily reading the full catalog. Rewrite output is fixed at four sections, the fourth being a second-pass audit that re-reads its own output and is declared the deliverable; iteration is capped at N=2 with a stated reason (a third pass costs a full regeneration and rarely finds more). Orthogonal axes compose by a narrowest-wins rule: checkable `mechanics` beat `--voice`, which beats a config's `register`, which beats `--context` (SKILL.md:130). The interesting half is the constraint on the editor rather than on the text: SKILL.md:201-217 forbids *adding* seven things the text did not already contain — fake first person, manufactured stakes, forced contrarianism, performed candor, em-dash theatrics, staccato conversion, invented specifics — with the rule "you may subtract and sharpen, you may not add", justified because provenance is something no pattern can see. Around that sits the evaluation layer: `scripts/fp-measure.js` scores a hash-only corpus where ground truth is *provenance, not a judge* (pre-LLM dated human text, so every flag on it is a false positive by construction), reporting FPR/TPR with Wilson intervals, threshold-free ROC-AUC via the Mann-Whitney U identity with ties credited a half, and per-category **lift** = machine firing rate / human firing rate, split by register, source and generating model. `scripts/self-scan.js` turns the detector on the repo's own docs and publishes two columns — raw and exemption-applied — with per-file budgets that only move down, gated in CI. `detector/validate.js` is a before/after preservation gate that makes the skill's prose promises executable.
measures:
Yes, genuinely — and it is the rare case where the answer is not "nothing". But it measures a different axis than we do, and it is honest that the axis we care about is untouched.

What it measures: (a) how well its own score separates machine text from human text, and (b) whether a rewrite destroyed content it had no business touching.

What it found, published in `corpus/README.md:136-199` against 875 human and 779 machine paragraphs: pooled paragraph ROC-AUC **0.501 — a coin flip**; document level 0.623. At score>=5, 4.2% FPR (95% CI 3.1-5.8) against 7.2% TPR. Three self-indicting findings: the 0-100 scale uses a tenth of its range (no paragraph of either class scored above 11); the 112-entry vocabulary table — the thing the README leads with — has a **lift of 0.9**, i.e. it fires slightly more often on human writing than machine writing; and the em-dash rule is **inverted at lift 0.2**, so on this corpus an em dash is evidence the text is human. The single strong discriminator in the whole engine is `uniformity` (rhythm) at **11.7x**. Verbatim: "the composite score cannot reliably separate machine text from human text."

The ground-truth design is the part worth copying: `corpus/README.md:11-23` — every document was written by a person, so every flag is a false positive by construction; "no labelling step, no judge, and no model in the loop: the ground truth is provenance." The corpus is hash-only (sha256 in `corpus/manifest.json`, text never committed, `corpus.js verify` fails loudly on mismatch rather than re-recording). I re-derived two of its claims from the manifest independently: exactly 9 public-domain works dated 1788-1907 at 6,000 words each, and 25 maintainer blog posts (27 blog/technical-blog entries minus Faraday-1861 and Franklin-1791) — both match the prose.

It also has a **publication gate** (`corpus/README.md:229-234`): no number enters the README, a release note or a social post until each claim cell has n>=100, a confidence interval, and more than one register people write in today. The gate is currently *failing* on the register test, and the repo therefore keeps its own FPR out of the README. That is the strongest signal of seriousness in the whole repo.

What it explicitly does NOT measure, `PROOF.md:205-206`: "The skill is documented as a writing-quality tool, and none of this touches whether its edits improve prose." No reader, no comprehension, no question-answering. Its objective function is "does this read as machine-written"; ours is "can a reader answer the question".

transferable.approach: Mechanical preservation gate on every rewrite: a before/after diff that ERRORS when the rewrite touched fenced code, YAML frontmatter, a blockquote, a table cell, inline code, a URL, a file path, or heading count/nesting — and WARNS on dropped figures or >40% word shrink. Carve-outs exist for edits the skill itself instructs (AI utm_source params stripped from both sides before comparing; heading text reworded is a warning, heading structure an error), on the stated grounds that a validator firing on its own skill's instructions would be turned off within a day.

transferable.approach: Per-category LIFT as a rule-pruning ruler: a rule earns its place only by separating the two classes. lift = firing rate on class A / firing rate on class B; below 1.0 the rule is firing more on the class you did not intend. Published as a table alongside the headline number, even when it indicts the flagship feature.
transferable.whereItLives: scripts/fp-measure.js:181-185 (the discrimination computation), reported at :242-247; the resulting table in corpus/README.md:170-181
transferable.whyItMightWork: This is the most method-shaped steal and the closest thing in this repo to terse's own logic. terse already measures per-question right/wrong and classifies failures as lie/placement/findability. Lift turns that into a verdict on each WRITING RULE: for each fixed rule in revise, compute the rate at which it fires on passages implicated in a wrong answer versus passages implicated in a right one. Rules at lift<1 are decoration. This is precisely the ruler that killed five published standards in our own bake-off, generalized from whole-standard granularity to per-rule granularity — and this repo's own run shows it works on the author's favourite feature (vocabulary table, lift 0.9) rather than only on strawmen.

weaknesses:
Four, the first two severe.

**1. The measurement indicts the product and the product did not change.** The corpus says the 112-entry vocabulary table has lift 0.9 (fires more on human writing) and the em-dash rule is inverted at lift 0.2. `corpus/README.md:208-211` then declines to prune: "It does not license a rewrite of the pattern list either … `delve` is still worth replacing." That may be defensible as writing advice, but it means the catalog's size is justified by taste while its discriminative claim has been measured and failed. The README still sells "112-entry word replacement table" and a pattern-category count as headline features (policed for drift across four external surfaces by `.ssot.yaml`), while the 0.501 number lives one link away in PROOF.md and appears nowhere in README.md.

**2. Ratio of prescription to measurement is roughly 300 KB to 30 KB.** 95 KB catalog + 127 KB engine + 133 KB engine tests against ~25 KB of actual measurement (`fp-measure.js`, `self-scan.js`, `validate.js`, `corpus.js`). Read by bulk it is a rule collection; read by its best files it is a method. Lifting it wholesale would reinstall exactly the failure mode our own bake-off found — a standard that produces audits rather than rewriting.

**3. Calibration defect the repo names itself.** The 0-100 scale uses a tenth of its range; no paragraph of either class scored above 11, so every ordinary paragraph lands in "Minimal AI signals" regardless of who wrote it. Cause is mechanical: category weights run 2-12 and rawScore is divided by max(1, log2(words/50)), halving a 200-word paragraph (`corpus/README.md:160-167`).

**4. The machine half of the corpus is stale and the repo says so.** HC3 is December-2022 ChatGPT only; RAID is 2024 and a different task shape (in-domain continuation, not "write a LinkedIn post"). Nothing has seen a 2026 model. Their own framing: an upper bound on performance, not an estimate of it. They refuse to generate positives locally, on the reasoning that doing so would measure the prompting of someone who knows the pattern list.

**Collision to watch for terse specifically.** The objective function is different. This repo optimizes "does not read as machine-written"; terse optimizes "a fresh reader answers the question right". Those can pull apart: a document can score 0 on this detector and still fail every reader question (the repo concedes this at PROOF.md:100-103 — "Prose can be hollow, structurally uniform, and entirely free of tells"). Do not import the catalog as a revise pass. Import the three rulers and the gate.

**One item for the already-rejected ledger, found not recommended.** README.md:432-439 explicitly *defers* CI style-gating to Vale rather than competing with it, names Vale's ports of proselint/write-good/alex, and frames the two tools as doing different jobs. So the prose-linter approach appears here as a neighbour the author routes around, which is consistent with our own rejection rather than a challenge to it. Hard per-sentence word limits and Diataxis do not appear at all.
